opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think one of the underappreciated things about the way technology usually enters the world is that it comes in stages, and those stages do a lot of work for us that we don't really notice. When a new capability arrives gradually, society gets to see the early, weaker versions first. We get to observe how they fail, what people use them for, what goes wrong at small scale, and we have time to build up the institutions, norms, laws, and technical safeguards that let us live with the more powerful versions later on.

Recursive self-improvement threatens to collapse all of that. If you have AI systems that can substantially speed up the research that produces the next generation of AI systems, then you might go from roughly human-level capabilities to something far beyond that in a period of months or even weeks rather than years or decades. And what you lose in that compression is precisely the intermediate stages, the systems that are a bit more capable than today's but not yet transformative, which would otherwise act as warning shots and as testing grounds.

So there are a few distinct dangers here. One is just epistemic: we'd have very little opportunity to learn about how these systems behave before the stakes become extremely high. Alignment techniques that work on one generation might break on the next, and if the generations are flying past, we may not notice until it's too late.

A second is institutional. Governments, regulators, and international bodies move slowly, sometimes for good reasons. They need time for deliberation and to build consensus. If the technology outpaces them by years, then the critical decisions effectively get made by whoever happens to be running the lab where this takes off, without any real democratic input or oversight.

And a third is about concentration of power. If one actor manages to get into that loop first, a modest lead could turn into an enormous one very quickly. That's destabilizing in itself, because it creates strong incentives to race and to cut corners on safety in order to be the one who gets there first.

So I'd put it this way: the gradualness of technological change is a kind of safety mechanism that humanity has always relied on without really naming it. Recursive self-improvement is dangerous partly because it could remove that mechanism at exactly the moment we'd need it most.

r001.rationale: The response says gradual development lets society observe failures and learn, but does not state that society is poor at predicting technologies’ effects before they arrive.

r002.rationale: It explains that skipping intermediate stages removes opportunities to observe failures and harms at small scale before the stakes become extremely high.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the key thing is that the intermediate stages are where society actually learns how to live with a technology. When a new capability arrives gradually, you get a whole series of smaller shocks, and each one gives people time to respond: regulators notice a problem and write rules, companies develop norms, researchers discover failure modes in systems that aren't yet powerful enough to be catastrophic, and the public forms views about what they're willing to accept. That's roughly how we've muddled through with most transformative technologies. It hasn't been elegant, but the feedback loop between capability and governance has mostly held.

Recursive self-improvement threatens to collapse that loop. If a system can improve its own capabilities, and those improvements make it better at improving itself, you could go from "quite impressive but manageable" to "far beyond human level" in a span of months or even weeks. And the problem isn't just that the jump is big, it's that you skip all the stages where we'd normally be learning. We wouldn't have had systems at the level just below that to study, to make mistakes with, to build institutions around. All of the accumulated wisdom we'd want for dealing with a very powerful system simply wouldn't exist yet.

There's also a concentration problem. In a gradual world, lots of actors have time to catch up, and power stays somewhat distributed. In a fast takeoff, whoever happens to be in front when the acceleration begins could end up with a decisive lead, maybe one that's never overtaken. That's dangerous even if the people involved have good intentions, because it removes the checks and balances that we normally rely on, and it puts enormous weight on one group getting everything right the first time.

And finally there's the alignment side. Our techniques for making systems safe and understanding what they're doing are developed and tested on the systems we currently have. If capabilities jump several levels at once, those techniques may simply not transfer, and we'd be discovering that in the worst possible circumstances, with a system already more capable than us. So when I say skipping the intermediate stages is dangerous, I really mean that those stages aren't wasted time. They're the time in which humanity does the thinking, the arguing, and the institution-building that a transition this significant actually requires.

r001.rationale: The response says society learns to live with technology as it develops, but does not state that society is poor at predicting new technologies’ effects before they arrive.

r002.rationale: It explains that intermediate systems let researchers discover failure modes and let society respond while systems are still manageable, before a jump to catastrophic capability.

astra-6.text:
Well, one reason is that those intermediate stages give us opportunities to learn. As AI systems become more capable, we get to see what goes wrong, how people use them, and whether our approaches to keeping them safe actually work. Society also gets time to adapt — to develop institutions and rules for dealing with these new capabilities.

With recursive self-improvement, you could have a system that becomes good enough at improving its own design that it rapidly makes itself much more capable, including at making further improvements. Then you might move through those intermediate stages very quickly. We could go from systems that are relatively manageable to something much more powerful without having had the experience we were counting on to learn how to handle it.

And that’s particularly worrying if the first really serious failure is one we can’t recover from. Learning by trial and error is a very powerful approach, but it depends on surviving the errors. So the concern isn’t simply that progress would be fast. It’s that the growth in capabilities could outpace our ability to understand and control those capabilities.

r001.rationale: The response discusses learning from failures as systems develop, but does not state that society is poor at predicting technological effects before they arrive.

r002.rationale: It says intermediate stages let society see what goes wrong while systems are relatively manageable, and warns that skipping them could leave society without experience handling failures before a serious, unrecoverable one.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, one reason is that those intermediate stages are opportunities to learn. If AI becomes more capable gradually, we get to see what kinds of problems arise, try out solutions, and develop institutions that can deal with them. We might discover that some of our proposed safety measures don’t work, but discover that while the consequences are still manageable.

With recursive self-improvement, there’s the possibility that a system becomes capable enough to improve its own design, and those improvements make it better at making further improvements. If that process happens very quickly, we could move from systems that are relatively limited to systems that vastly exceed human capabilities without much time in between.

And then we’d be confronting the hardest version of the problem with very little practical experience. Our technical safeguards and our social institutions would have to work under conditions we hadn’t had a chance to study. So the concern isn’t simply that progress is fast. It’s that we might lose the opportunity to learn from smaller mistakes before a mistake could have irreversible consequences.

r001.rationale: The response says gradual development would let society observe problems and learn, but it does not state that society is poor at predicting new technologies’ effects before they arrive.

r002.rationale: The response explains that gradual stages allow society to learn from problems while consequences are manageable, whereas skipping them could leave little experience before irreversible consequences.
